title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Explain the load-support and controlled-motion functions of a suspension spring-damper assembly.
student: Based on the automotive application shown, explain the primary mechanical function of the suspension spring-damper assembly.
instructor: The suspension supports vertical vehicle load while allowing controlled relative motion between the wheel-side suspension and the vehicle body. The coil spring provides elastic compliance and stores/releases energy, while the damper controls oscillatory motion.
gradingNotes: Students should focus on load support and controlled suspension motion. Detailed vehicle-dynamics discussion is not required for this Solid Mechanics problem.

title: External Loading
learningObjectives: Identify the dominant external loading represented in the simplified suspension model.
student: What type of external loading acts on the suspension during vehicle operation, and what loading direction is most relevant to the simplified problem?
instructor: The suspension carries forces transmitted between the wheel-side assembly and the vehicle body due to vehicle weight and road input. For the simplified problem, the dominant response is represented by a vertical or axial load acting through the compliant suspension system.
gradingNotes: Students should identify the dominant vertical load transfer without introducing notation from the later instructor model.

title: Supports and Restraints
learningObjectives: Describe how suspension connections transfer load while permitting working travel.
student: Identify where the suspension spring-damper assembly is connected to the vehicle and explain, in general terms, what relative motion those connections allow or restrain.
instructor: The spring-damper assembly is connected between the vehicle body or chassis and the wheel-side suspension structure. The connections transfer load between these parts while allowing the suspension to move vertically over its working travel.
gradingNotes: The goal is physical interpretation of the real suspension. Do not require students to identify the rigid plates or point labels that appear only in the later equivalent model.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace the dominant vertical load path through the real suspension system.
student: Trace the dominant vertical load path through the suspension from the wheel-side suspension structure to the vehicle body.
instructor: A suitable load path is from the wheel-side suspension and control arm into the spring-damper mounting region, through the compliant spring-damper assembly, and into the vehicle body or chassis. The same path transfers load in the opposite direction depending on the chosen free body.
gradingNotes: Students should describe the real load path in physical terms before any equivalent-model notation is introduced.

title: Components Controlling Compliance
learningObjectives: Identify the components that control suspension compliance in a simplified model.
student: Which parts of the suspension system are most important when considering vertical compliance or relative displacement under load?
instructor: The coil spring is the primary compliant component. Elastic deformation of load-carrying structural members and attachments can also contribute to the total relative displacement, although many surrounding components may be treated as comparatively rigid in a simplified model.
gradingNotes: The emphasis is deformation and stiffness. Students do not need to identify every visible suspension component.

title: Relevant Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Select the deformation mechanisms needed to predict a quasi-static spacing change.
student: What deformation mechanisms should be considered if the engineering concern is the change in spacing between two suspension reference locations under a slowly applied load?
instructor: The main deformation mechanisms are spring compression and elastic deformation of the load-carrying members. Their relative motions must be combined through compatibility to determine the overall change in spacing. Velocity-dependent damping is not part of the quasi-static base model.
gradingNotes: This question introduces the mechanics needed later without giving students the instructor-model labels or equations.

title: Relevant Geometric and Material Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify the loading, geometry, material, and member-count inputs controlling compliance.
student: What loading, geometric, and material characteristics would you expect to control the compliance of the simplified suspension model?
instructor: Relevant characteristics include the applied load magnitude, spring stiffness, member lengths, cross-sectional dimensions, elastic modulus of the load-carrying members, and the number of parallel members sharing the load.
gradingNotes: Students should identify physical dependencies conceptually. Specific symbols, formulas, and numerical values are introduced only with the instructor reference model.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Create a one-dimensional equivalent model that preserves the dominant compliant load path.
student:
Convert the real suspension system into a simplified one-dimensional Mechanics of Materials model that preserves the dominant compliant load path. Represent the spring as a linear spring, represent selected load-carrying members as axial members, treat the main attachment structures as rigid, and show the applied load and the reference separation whose change is to be evaluated.

Student model: Insert or draw the simplified model and free-body / deformation diagram here.
instructor: A suitable student model replaces the detailed automotive geometry with an equivalent spring-and-axial-member assembly. The model should capture spring compression, elastic elongation of the load-carrying members, and the compatibility needed to determine the change in separation between two reference locations.
gradingNotes: Students are not expected to reproduce the instructor reference geometry exactly. The goal is to demonstrate the transition from the real automotive system to an analyzable compliance model.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State the assumptions supporting the spring-and-axial-member idealization.
student: State the assumptions needed to convert the automotive suspension into a simplified quasi-static spring-and-axial-member model.
instructor: Typical assumptions include: the applied loading is quasi-static and predominantly vertical; the spring is linear; the main attachment structures are rigid; the axial members are linearly elastic; deformations are small; loading is concentric; identical parallel members share load equally; and bending, shear deformation, friction, thread/contact compliance, and velocity-dependent damper forces are neglected in the base model.
gradingNotes: The essential assumptions are quasi-static loading, linear spring behavior, rigid attachment structures, axial member deformation, and equal load sharing for identical parallel members.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the equilibrium, deformation, and compatibility steps needed to determine reference separation.
student: Before performing numerical calculations, describe the sequence required to determine the change in reference separation using an equivalent spring-and-axial-member model.
instructor: A complete plan is to determine internal load sharing from equilibrium, calculate spring compression, calculate axial elongation of the load-carrying members, combine the compatible deformation contributions, determine the resulting reference separation, and identify which contribution dominates the response.
gradingNotes: The detailed point labels, member dimensions, and numerical data needed for this sequence are introduced in the instructor reference model that follows.

title: Boundary / Loading Conditions from Instructor Diagram
learningObjectives: Interpret the loading and mechanical idealizations in the instructor reference model.
student: From the instructor diagram, identify the loading condition and the main mechanical idealizations.
instructor: The assembly is subjected to equal and opposite tensile loads P. The plates A, B, and C are rigid. The spring is linear with stiffness k. The side bolts and central rod deform axially. The system response is evaluated by tracking how deformation changes the distance d between C and E.
gradingNotes: This question replaces a standard support-reaction question because the problem is an axial assembly rather than a beam/frame.

title: Unknown Internal Loads and Load Sharing
learningObjectives: Determine spring, coupling-rod, and side-bolt forces using equilibrium and symmetry.
student: Identify the force in the spring, the force in the coupling rod segment, and the force in each side bolt.
instructor: The spring force is P = {{spring_force_kip}} kip. The coupling rod segment carries P = {{spring_rod_force_kip}} kip in tension. The two side bolts share the load equally, so each side bolt carries P/2 = {{spring_bolt_force_kip}} kip in tension.
gradingNotes: The equal sharing of load in the two side bolts follows from symmetry and identical bolt geometry.

title: Spring Compression
learningObjectives: Calculate compression using the linear spring force-displacement relation.
student: Calculate the compression of the spring.
instructor: δs = P/k = {{P}}/{{k}} = {{spring_compression_in}} in. This compression increases the distance between points C and E in the final configuration.
gradingNotes: Students should use kip and kip/in consistently.

title: Coupling Rod Elongation
learningObjectives: Calculate the axial elongation of the active coupling-rod segment.
student: Calculate the elongation of the active coupling rod segment.
instructor:
Ab = π({{d_b}} in)2/4 = {{spring_member_area_in2}} in2. The rod elongation is

δrod = PLE/(AbEs) = ({{P}} kip)({{L_E}} in)/[{{spring_member_area_in2}} in2({{E_s}} kip/in2)] = {{spring_rod_elongation_in}} in.
gradingNotes: This deformation contributes to increasing d because the loaded eye E moves away from C.

title: Side-Bolt Elongation
learningObjectives: Calculate the elongation of identical side bolts that share load in parallel.
student: Calculate the elongation of each side bolt.
instructor:
Each side bolt carries P/2 = {{spring_bolt_force_kip}} kip. The side-bolt elongation is

δbolt = (P/2)Lb/(AbEs) = ({{spring_bolt_force_kip}} kip)({{L_b}} in)/[{{spring_member_area_in2}} in2({{E_s}} kip/in2)] = {{spring_bolt_elongation_in}} in.
gradingNotes: The two bolts have the same elongation because they are identical and loaded symmetrically.

title: Final Distance d
learningObjectives: Combine compatible deformation contributions to determine the final C-to-E distance.
student: Determine the final distance d between C and E after loading.
instructor: The increase in distance is Δd = δs + δrod + δbolt = {{spring_compression_in}} + {{spring_rod_elongation_in}} + {{spring_bolt_elongation_in}} = {{spring_distance_increase_in}} in. Therefore, d = d0 + Δd = {{d0}} + {{spring_distance_increase_in}} = {{spring_final_distance_in}} in.
gradingNotes: This is the main numerical result. Students should explain why the deformation contributions are added.

title: Stiffness-Based Interpretation
learningObjectives: Relate the dominant displacement contribution to relative component stiffness.
student: Which deformation contribution dominates the change in distance d, and why?
instructor: The spring compression dominates because δs = {{spring_compression_in}} in is much larger than the steel-member elongations, which are approximately {{spring_rod_elongation_in}} in and {{spring_bolt_elongation_in}} in. The spring has much lower stiffness than the steel members.
gradingNotes: This helps students connect stiffness values to physical deformation.

title: Stiffness-Based Modification
learningObjectives: Recommend a mechanics-based modification that reduces final displacement.
student: If the final distance d must be reduced, identify a mechanics-based design modification.
instructor: Possible modifications include increasing spring stiffness k, increasing bolt/rod diameter, reducing the active member lengths, reducing the applied load, or changing the assembly geometry. The most effective single change is usually increasing k because the spring compression dominates the displacement.
gradingNotes: Keep this as a limited mechanics recommendation, not a full redesign.

title: Strength Factor of Safety
learningObjectives: Recognize when the supplied data do not support a strength factor-of-safety calculation.
student: Do not compute strength factor of safety unless allowable stresses or material strengths are provided.
instructor: The base problem asks for displacement, not strength safety. If allowable stress data are added, axial stresses in the coupling rod and side bolts could be checked.
gradingNotes: Instructor-only extension.

title: Stability or Buckling Check
learningObjectives: Explain why buckling is not part of the base tension-member analysis.
student: Evaluate buckling only if a slender compression member is identified and relevant geometry/end conditions are provided.
instructor: Buckling is not part of the base problem. The side bolts and central rod are in tension; the spring compresses but is modeled only by its stiffness k.
gradingNotes: Do not include as a student-facing question unless the learning objective is explicitly about why stability is not relevant.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Summarize the equivalent-model response and relate it cautiously to suspension compliance.
student: Use the mechanics results to summarize the response of the equivalent model and relate the dominant deformation contribution to suspension compliance.
instructor: Under the specified {{P}}-kip tensile load, the equivalent model gives a final distance d = {{spring_final_distance_in}} in. Spring compression is the dominant deformation contribution, so the modeled compliance is governed primarily by spring stiffness. This conclusion applies to the simplified quasi-static model; the full vehicle suspension also contains geometric, damping, bushing, and other effects that are outside the scope of the present MEEN 305 analysis.
gradingNotes: The recommendation should return to the automotive suspension context while clearly distinguishing the equivalent mechanics model from the full vehicle system.
